name: Zen Buddhism
era: 6th century China; 12th century Japan to today
line: Sit, work and eat with full attention.

quote.text: To study the Buddha Way is to study the self. To study the self is to forget the self.

quotes.text: In the beginner’s mind there are many possibilities, but in the expert’s there are few.
Have you eaten your rice porridge? Then you had better wash your bowl.
My miraculous power and spiritual activity: drawing water and carrying firewood.

words.usage: Za is to sit, zen is meditation. The heart of the practice.
Sōtō practice: sitting with no object and no goal.
A story or question from the old masters that logic cannot settle.
Zhaozhou’s answer when asked if a dog has Buddha nature. The first kōan for many students.
Seeing things as they are. Not a possession and not an ending.
A first glimpse of awakening, to be deepened by practice.
Meeting each thing as if for the first time.
The mind not caught on anything; acting without the self in the way.
Sweeping, cooking and gardening done as meditation.
Slow walking between periods of sitting.
Literally, gathering the mind. Several days of near-continuous sitting.
You bow on entering and on leaving.
Sit on the front third so the knees can settle.
A gesture of respect and of two becoming one.
A title for a senior Zen teacher.
One of the three treasures, with Buddha and Dharma.

words.meaning: The teaching; the way things are
words.usage: Both what the Buddha taught and the truth it points to.
The set of nested bowls, and the formal way of eating from them.
Dōgen wrote that the role demands an awakened mind.
Where a student presents their understanding.
A presentation of the teaching, not a lecture about it.
A flat stick used on the shoulders to wake a drowsy sitter, often on request.
Breath and attention settle here in zazen.
Dōgen’s word for the mind in zazen: neither thinking nor suppressing thought.
Everything is passing. Dōgen: impermanence is itself Buddha nature.
Nothing has a fixed, separate self. Sanskrit: śūnyatā.
Brushed in a single stroke. It shows the mind of the moment it was made.

words.meaning: Beauty in the plain, worn and imperfect
words.usage: An aesthetic shaped by Zen and the tea ceremony.
From the way of tea: this gathering will never happen again.
Attention that stays after the action is finished.

words.meaning: A short verse recited during daily acts
words.usage: There are verses for waking, washing and eating.

words.meaning: One who vows to awaken with all beings
words.usage: The ideal of Mahāyāna Buddhism, to which Zen belongs.

practices.name: Zazen
practices.instructions: Sit on the front third of a firm cushion, or upright on a chair with your feet flat. Lengthen the spine, tuck the chin a little, rest the left hand in the right with the thumbs lightly touching. Keep the eyes half open, lowered to the floor a metre ahead. Breathe through the nose and count each out-breath from one to ten, then begin again. When you drift, come back to one without comment.
practices.why: Dōgen called zazen the dharma gate of ease and joy, and insisted it is not a means to awakening but awakening practised. The posture itself is the teaching.
variations: Once counting is steady, drop it and simply follow the breath.
Sit ten minutes on a day that is full, rather than skipping.
Sit facing a plain wall, as Sōtō students do.

practices.name: Samu
practices.instructions: Choose one physical task: sweep a floor, wash the dishes, weed a bed. Do it in silence with no audio and no hurry. Give the broom, the cloth or the bowl the same attention you gave the breath. When you finish, put every tool back where it lives, and notice how the room feels.
practices.why: Baizhang’s rule for Chan monasteries: a day without work is a day without food. In Zen there is no line between practice and chores.
variations: Clean one thing nobody will notice.
Cook breakfast as samu.
Fifteen minutes of care for a shared space.

practices.name: Make the bed like a monk
practices.instructions: Make your bed as if it were the first act of the day, because it is. Smooth the sheet with your palm, square the corners, and set the pillow with care. Do it slowly and in silence. Do not check anything else until it is done. A made bed is a small, true thing you can finish before breakfast.
practices.why: Zen teachers often begin with the smallest tasks, because the mind that is careful with a blanket is careful with a life. Nothing needs to be saved for later.
variations: Open the window first and let the air in.
Make the guest bed, or someone else’s.
Bow lightly to the finished bed.

practices.name: Just washing the face
practices.instructions: When you wash your face, only wash your face. Feel the water on your skin, its temperature, the sound in the basin, the towel. When a thought starts planning the day, notice it and come back to the cloth in your hands. Take a full minute. Come out of the bathroom a little more awake than you went in.
practices.why: Zhaozhou’s answer to a monk who asked for teaching was to ask if he had eaten, and then to tell him to wash his bowl. Zen practice lives in just this, in water and in cloth.
variations: Wash your hands as slowly as a tea master.
Wash with cold water and nothing else.
Say thank you silently to the water.

practices.name: A cup of hot water
practices.instructions: Pour plain hot water into a cup you like. Hold it in both hands and let the warmth move up your wrists. Drink it slowly, standing or sitting, with no screen. Monks often drink it, called sayu. Notice what a plain thing tastes like, and how little you needed to add.
practices.why: Sayu is the simplest tea in Zen: no leaves, no ceremony, only warmth and attention. It makes a good bridge between sleep and the day.
variations: Add one thin slice of ginger.
Drink it on a step outside.
Make a cup for someone else without telling them.

practices.name: Ten breaths at the window
practices.instructions: When you have no time for zazen, stand or sit at a window and count ten slow breaths, in and out, looking at the sky or the street. At each breath, name nothing and fix nothing. On ten, stop and turn to your day. It is the shortest sitting there is, and it is still a sitting.
practices.why: Sitting does not need a cushion or an hour. Teachers say a few breaths of full attention are worth more than a long sit with a wandering mind.
variations: Do it with the window open and listen.
Do it before you open your phone.
Do ten more if the first ten fly by.

practices.name: Silent meal
practices.instructions: Eat one meal without speaking, reading or a screen. Pause before the first bite and think about where the food came from. Take modest portions and finish everything. Put your utensils down between mouthfuls. Wash your bowl as soon as you are done.
practices.why: Formal Zen meals, ōryōki, are eaten in silence from nested bowls that are wiped clean with tea or water, which is then drunk. Nothing is wasted.
variations: Recite a short verse of thanks before eating.
Eat with one bowl and one spoon.
Share a silent meal with someone.

practices.name: Walking meditation
practices.instructions: Choose a path of ten to twenty steps, indoors or out. Walk very slowly, matching each step to a breath. Feel the heel, the ball of the foot, the lifting. When you reach the end, pause, turn, and walk back. If the mind wanders, return to the soles of your feet.
practices.why: In Zen halls, walking meditation (kinhin) sits between periods of zazen, so that stillness does not stay in the legs but enters ordinary movement.
variations: Walk with hands folded at the chest.
Walk outside along one fixed route.
Five minutes before every meal.

practices.name: Clear one surface
practices.instructions: Choose one surface, a desk, a table, a shelf, a windowsill, and clear it completely. Put away what belongs elsewhere, wipe it down, and leave on it only what you truly use. Step back and look at the space you have made. Do not start another surface. One is enough.
practices.why: Sōji, cleaning, is a daily Zen practice done by everyone, including the teacher. An empty surface is a visible picture of an uncluttered mind.
variations: Clear the surface you look at most.
Leave one thing on it, on purpose, because it is beautiful.
Clear someone else’s surface, with their leave.

practices.name: Do one thing
practices.instructions: Choose one task and give it your whole attention for twenty minutes: phone away, one window open on the screen, no snacks. When your hand reaches for something else, notice the reach and stay. When the time is up, stop and look at what you have done. One thing at a time, really.
practices.why: The first rule of this Onda is one thing at a time. Zen calls this just this: when you walk, walk; when you eat, eat. Attention is the practice.
variations: Choose the task you have put off longest.
Do it standing up.
Do it as an offering to someone you care for.

practices.name: Carry a kōan for a walk
practices.instructions: Take a kōan for a walk: Does a dog have Buddha-nature? Joshu said Mu. Say it once, then walk with it, not trying to solve it. When an answer pops up, let it go and walk on. After ten minutes, notice what the question has done to your mind, however little.
practices.why: A kōan is not a riddle to be answered but a question to be lived with. The Gateless Gate opens with Mu, the most famous one, and students carry it for years.
variations: What is the sound of one hand?
Before your parents were born, what was your face?
Pick any plain question: Who is walking?

practices.name: Three minutes of sound
practices.instructions: Sit or stand and listen to whatever sound there is for three minutes, rain, wind, a fridge, traffic, as if it were music someone had written just for you. Do not name the sounds, only hear them. When your attention snaps to a story, return to the next sound. Let the last one fade.
practices.why: Zen teachers point to hearing as a doorway into the present: sound is always here and always now. John Cage, a student of D. T. Suzuki, built a whole piece out of it.
variations: Close your eyes.
Listen in a place you pass every day.
Listen for the quietest sound of all.

practices.name: Tea and stillness
practices.instructions: Heat the water, warm the cup, make the tea and carry it to a quiet place. Hold the cup in both hands. Drink it while doing nothing else. When the cup is empty, sit for a few more breaths, then wash and dry it.
practices.why: Eisai brought tea seeds from China with Zen in 1191, partly to keep monks awake. The tea ceremony grew from that habit into a discipline of its own.
variations: Whisk a bowl of matcha.
Plain hot water, as monks often drink.
Sit outside with your tea and watch the light go.

practices.name: Write a haiku
practices.instructions: Look back over today and find one small moment: a sound, a light, a smell. Write it in three short lines, roughly five, seven and five beats, and include a word that tells the season, such as frost, cicada or blossom. Do not explain or comment. Leave the poem as plain as the moment.
practices.why: Bashō, who walked and wrote in the Zen spirit, held that a haiku is just what is happening in this place at this moment. The season word ties a small thing to the great turning.
variations: Write it by hand on a scrap and leave it somewhere.
Write three, then keep one.
Read it aloud to someone.

practices.name: Copy a line by hand
practices.instructions: Choose one line from a book, a poem or a teaching that struck you this week. Copy it slowly by hand, in your best writing, one stroke at a time. Let the copying be the practice, not the line. When you finish, read it once and leave the page where you will see it tomorrow.
practices.why: Copying sutras, shakyo, is an old devotional practice in Japan. The slowness of the brush or pen is the point: the hand teaches the mind to stay.
variations: Copy the shortest sentence you know by heart.
Copy with a brush pen or a fountain pen.
Copy a line by someone you disagree with.

practices.name: Bow to close the day
practices.instructions: Before you go to bed, stand at the door of the room where you spent the day, or at your sitting spot, and put your palms together. Bow slightly, thanking the day, the place and the people in it. Hold the bow for one breath, then turn out the light. Small ceremonies make a day feel finished.
practices.why: The gasshō bow is how Zen students greet and leave the hall, each other and their own cushions. It marks the edges of an experience so it does not smear into the next.
variations: Bow to the empty chair or the cushion.
Bow to the kitchen after a meal.
Bow to each person at home if they allow.

practices.name: Where were you here?
practices.instructions: Think back over the day and find three moments when you were truly here, fully in what you were doing: a mouthful, a step, a conversation. Write each in one line. If you cannot find three, write one and notice that this is also a finding. Do not judge. Just count.
practices.why: Zen is not about big experiences. It asks you to notice the small times when mind and body were in the same place, so you can find that place again.
variations: Write only one moment, in detail.
Write the moments you missed, and what pulled you away.
Tell someone aloud instead of writing.

practices.name: Wash the bowl
practices.instructions: After your evening meal, wash your own bowl, plate and cup slowly and in silence. Feel the water, the sponge, the shape of each thing, and set it to dry with care. Do not rush to the next thing. Leave the sink clean. When it is done, notice that nothing remains to be done here.
practices.why: A monk asked Zhaozhou for teaching. Have you eaten your rice porridge? Then you had better wash your bowl. In Zen, the end of a meal is part of the meal.
variations: Wash for someone else too.
Wash by hand, even if there is a dishwasher.
Leave a clean cloth folded neatly on the side.

practices.name: Moon viewing
practices.instructions: On a clear night, make tea, step outside and look at the moon. Sit for fifteen minutes and do nothing but look, drink, and breathe. Japan calls this tsukimi. If it is cloudy, sit by a window and look at where the moon would be. Come in feeling that the moon has been sitting with you.
practices.why: Dōgen wrote of the moon reflected in a drop of dew: the whole moon fits in one drop. Moon viewing has been a quiet Japanese custom for centuries, with poems, tea and silence.
variations: Bring a friend and say nothing for ten minutes.
Write one line of poem about it.
Look at the moon and think of one person looking at the same one.

practices.name: Two sittings and a walk
practices.instructions: On a free morning, sit for twenty minutes, walk slowly for ten, then sit for twenty more. Keep silence from the moment you wake until you finish. No phone. It is a small sesshin, an intensive retreat, at home. Afterward eat something plain and notice how bright an ordinary room has become.
practices.why: In Zen halls, periods of sitting alternate with walking, and a retreat of many such rounds is called sesshin. One morning of it is enough to feel how much of the mind’s noise is optional.
variations: Do it with a friend in a shared silence.
Do it outside in a garden or park.
End with a bowl of rice porridge.

immersePlan.name: Read a short talk by Suzuki
immersePlan.text: Open the book anywhere. The talks are only a few pages. Read one slowly, then close it and sit for two minutes. Suzuki’s theme is beginner’s mind: many possibilities for the beginner, few for the expert.

immersePlan.name: Read Dōgen on the cook
immersePlan.text: Read a few lines of Dōgen’s Instructions for the Cook, written in 1237. It is about washing rice and caring for vegetables as if they were your own eyes. Then go and wash something with the same care.

immersePlan.name: Read a poem by Ryōkan
immersePlan.text: Read a few poems by the hermit Ryōkan, the monk who played ball with village children. Choose one and read it aloud, to yourself or someone else.

immersePlan.name: Watch Enlightenment Guaranteed
immersePlan.text: Put on Doris Dörrie’s comedy about two German brothers who end up in a Japanese monastery. It is funny and kind. Notice the ordinary chores and what they teach the brothers.

immersePlan.name: Watch a season in a mountain monastery
immersePlan.text: Watch Zen for Nothing, a quiet film about life at the working monastery of Antai-ji. Do not wait for a plot. Let the chores, the snow and the silence be the film.

immersePlan.name: Watch an almost silent film
immersePlan.text: Watch Bae Yong-kyun’s film of a Korean mountain monastery, with a child, a young monk and an old master. Little is said. Keep your phone away and see how long you can stay with a slow shot.

immersePlan.name: Listen to shakuhachi
immersePlan.text: Play the shakuhachi pieces once played by wandering monks as blown meditation. Sit for ten minutes with eyes half open and listen to the breath inside each note.

immersePlan.name: Hear the Heart Sutra chanted
immersePlan.text: Play a temple recording of the Heart Sutra. Follow the rhythm more than the words, and notice how it sounds when a whole room breathes together. Chant along softly if you like.

immersePlan.name: Sit through Cage’s silence
immersePlan.text: Set a timer for four minutes and thirty-three seconds and sit with a window open. Cage studied Zen with D. T. Suzuki. Count how many different sounds you hear, and which one you had not noticed before.

immersePlan.name: Look at the Ryōan-ji garden
immersePlan.text: Find a good photograph or film of the rock garden. There are fifteen stones, but from any one spot one is always hidden. Look for five minutes and ask what you are not seeing.

immersePlan.name: Look at Muqi’s six persimmons
immersePlan.text: Spend five minutes with the ink painting: six fruit in a row, some pale, some dark. Ask how so few strokes can feel complete. Then look at a piece of fruit in your own kitchen.

immersePlan.name: Draw an ensō
immersePlan.text: Draw a circle in one breath with a brush or a thick pen. Do not correct it. Draw five, and keep the one that is most honest. Zen painters say the circle shows the state of the mind that drew it.

immersePlan.name: Make a pot of okayu
immersePlan.text: Simmer a small cup of rice in five or six cups of water until it is soft, with a pinch of salt. Eat it slowly, as the monastery breakfast, and finish it all. Add one pickle if you have one.

immersePlan.name: Eat a plain temple meal
immersePlan.text: Make miso soup and a bowl of plain rice with one pickle. Eat in silence and take modest portions. Wipe the bowl clean with the last of your tea and drink that too.

immersePlan.name: Taste takuan
immersePlan.text: If you can find it, eat a slice or two of takuan, the yellow pickled radish said to be named for the Zen master Takuan Sōhō. If not, pickle thin slices of radish in salt and vinegar, and taste them tomorrow.

immersePlan.name: Whisk a bowl of matcha
immersePlan.text: Sift a little matcha into a warm bowl, add hot (not boiling) water, and whisk in a zigzag until frothy. Drink it in three or four sips and turn the bowl before you finish. A fork will do for a whisk.

immersePlan.name: Brew a pot of green tea
immersePlan.text: Let the water cool a little off the boil, pour it over the leaves, and wait about a minute. Drink the first cup slowly, and notice how the second cup tastes different from the first.

immersePlan.name: Drink hot water, sayu
immersePlan.text: Fill a cup you like with plain hot water and drink it slowly, doing nothing else. Monks often drink it. Notice that you can taste warmth.

immersePlan.name: Bow at every door today
immersePlan.text: Each time you go through a doorway today, pause and put your palms together for one breath, or just dip your head. A doorway becomes a small ceremony.

immersePlan.name: Wipe your bowl clean
immersePlan.text: At your next meal, finish everything and wipe the bowl with the last of your drink, then drink that too. It is the ōryōki habit: nothing wasted, nothing left for someone else to clean.

immersePlan.name: Clean together for ten minutes
immersePlan.text: Ask someone you live or work with to clean with you for ten minutes. In Zen temples sōji is done by everyone, teacher included. Put on music, or none, and say little.

immersePlan.name: Play a game of Go
immersePlan.text: Play a short game on a nine-by-nine board, in person or on a free online board. Place a stone and notice how a small decision spreads. If you are new, a free lesson takes ten minutes.

immersePlan.name: Walk the Tokaido
immersePlan.text: If you have the board game, play a round: you travel the old road from Kyoto to Edo and score for savouring things, not for racing. If not, take a walk and give yourself a point for each thing you stop to enjoy.

immersePlan.name: Play a round of karuta
immersePlan.text: Look up a few of the hundred classical poems (the Hyakunin Isshu) and play with a friend: one reads the first lines, the other grabs the card with the ending. It is played all over Japan at New Year.

immersePlan.name: Ring out the old year
immersePlan.text: On 31 December temple bells are struck 108 times to see out the passions. Any evening, strike a bowl or glass slowly, once for each worry you are putting down. Let each tone fade before the next.

immersePlan.name: Give a flower for the Buddha’s birthday
immersePlan.text: On 8 April, Hanamatsuri, people pour sweet tea over a small statue of the infant Buddha under a flowered canopy. Today, take a flower, or a sprig, and give it to someone with no reason.

immersePlan.name: Sit in a garden for twenty minutes
immersePlan.text: Find a garden, a rock garden or a quiet corner of a park and sit for twenty minutes. At Ryōan-ji people sit on a veranda and look at fifteen stones. Choose your own stones and stay until you stop counting.

immersePlan.name: Try beginner’s mind
immersePlan.text: Pick one thing you think you know well, a route, a drink, a person, and meet it again as if for the first time. Shoshin is Suzuki’s word for this mind. Write one thing you notice that you had not before.

immersePlan.name: Walk with the word Mu
immersePlan.text: Mu means no, not, without. Joshu said it when asked if a dog has Buddha-nature. Repeat it on a walk, not as an answer but as a pebble to carry. Notice when the mind stops asking.

immersePlan.name: Breathe into the hara
immersePlan.text: Hara is the belly, the centre where Zen places breath and balance. Put a hand below your navel and breathe into it ten times. Stand up and notice how a steadier centre changes the way you walk.

rules.text: One thing at a time. Really.
rules.why: Walk when you walk, eat when you eat. Divided attention is the habit this Onda exists to interrupt.

rules.text: Let silence open the day: no phone before you sit
rules.why: The first thing the mind meets sets its tone for the morning. Give it a few breaths of nothing before you give it the world.
Without chatter, a bowl of rice turns out to have flavour, weight and a whole history behind it.

rules.text: Leave every room cleaner than you found it
rules.why: Care for a place is care for everyone who comes after you. In Zen training, cleaning is practice, not chore.

rules.text: Waste nothing: a grain, a page, a minute
rules.why: Dōgen had the cook treat a single leaf of greens as the body of the Buddha. If a leaf deserves that, so does your next minute.
A small pause of respect, to the cushion, the meal or the work, marks it as practice and not just activity.

read.title: Zen Mind, Beginner’s Mind
read.creator: Shunryū Suzuki
read.why: Short talks by the founder of San Francisco Zen Center. The clearest way in.

read.title: Moon in a Dewdrop
read.creator: Dōgen, ed. Kazuaki Tanahashi
read.why: Selected writings, including Genjōkōan and instructions for zazen.

read.title: Instructions for the Cook
read.creator: Dōgen
read.why: Tenzo Kyōkun: how to wash rice with a whole heart.

read.title: The Gateless Gate
read.creator: Wumen Huikai
read.why: Forty-eight kōans with a master’s comments. Read one and stop.

read.title: The Platform Sutra
read.creator: Attributed to Huineng, trans. Red Pine
read.why: The illiterate woodcutter who became the Sixth Patriarch.

read.title: The Narrow Road to the Deep North
read.creator: Matsuo Bashō
read.why: A walking journal in prose and haiku by a poet steeped in Zen.

read.title: One Robe, One Bowl
read.creator: Ryōkan, trans. John Stevens
read.why: Poems of a hermit monk who played ball with village children.

read.title: The Three Pillars of Zen
read.creator: Philip Kapleau
read.why: Teaching, practice and first-hand accounts from a Japanese training hall.

read.title: The Book of Tea
read.creator: Okakura Kakuzō
read.why: How Zen shaped tea, architecture and the Japanese sense of beauty.

watch.title: Zen
watch.creator: Banmei Takahashi
watch.why: A film life of Dōgen, from China to the founding of Eihei-ji.

watch.title: Zen for Nothing
watch.creator: Werner Penzel
watch.why: A season at Antai-ji, a working Sōtō monastery in the mountains.

watch.title: Enlightenment Guaranteed
watch.creator: Doris Dörrie
watch.why: Two German brothers stumble into a Japanese monastery. Funny and honest.

watch.title: Why Has Bodhi-Dharma Left for the East?
watch.creator: Bae Yong-kyun
watch.why: Korean Sŏn rather than Japanese Zen, and almost wordless.

listen.title: A Bell Ringing in the Empty Sky
listen.creator: Gorō Yamaguchi
listen.why: Shakuhachi pieces once played by wandering monks as blown meditation.

listen.title: Heart Sutra chant
listen.creator: Any Sōtō or Rinzai temple recording
listen.why: Hannya Shingyō, chanted daily: form is emptiness, emptiness is form.

listen.title: Shunryū Suzuki talks
listen.creator: San Francisco Zen Center archive
listen.why: The original recordings behind Zen Mind, Beginner’s Mind.

listen.creator: John Cage
listen.why: Cage studied Zen with D. T. Suzuki. Four and a half minutes of whatever the room is doing.

art.title: Rock garden of Ryōan-ji
art.creator: Kyoto
art.why: Fifteen stones in raked gravel. From the veranda you can never see all of them at once.

art.title: Six Persimmons
art.creator: Muqi
art.why: Ink on paper, kept at Daitoku-ji. Almost nothing, and complete.

art.title: Splashed-Ink Landscape
art.creator: Sesshū Tōyō
art.why: A mountain made of a few wet strokes. Tokyo National Museum.

art.title: Pine Trees
art.creator: Hasegawa Tōhaku
art.why: Two folding screens that are mostly mist.

art.title: Circle, Triangle, Square
art.creator: Sengai Gibon
art.why: Three shapes and no explanation. Idemitsu Museum of Arts, Tokyo.

art.title: Ensō
art.creator: Any Zen calligrapher
art.why: Look at several. Each circle is a different mind.

eat.title: Rice porridge
eat.creator: Okayu, the monastery breakfast
eat.why: Rice simmered soft with water and a pinch of salt.

eat.title: Miso soup and rice
eat.creator: With one pickle
eat.why: One soup, one side: the basic temple meal.

eat.title: Shōjin ryōri
eat.creator: Buddhist temple cuisine
eat.why: Vegetables, tofu and sesame, with no meat, fish, onion or garlic.

eat.title: Sesame tofu
eat.creator: Goma-dōfu
eat.why: Ground sesame set with kudzu. A temple dish that takes patience to stir.

eat.title: Pickled daikon
eat.creator: Takuan
eat.why: By tradition named after the Zen master Takuan Sōhō.

drink.title: Matcha
drink.creator: Whisked powdered green tea
drink.why: The tea of the tea ceremony.

drink.title: Sencha or bancha
drink.creator: Everyday green tea
drink.why: Brewed with water just off the boil.

drink.title: Hot water
drink.creator: Sayu
drink.why: Plain, in a cup you like.

customs.title: Bow at the door
customs.creator: Gasshō
customs.why: Bring the palms together on entering and leaving the place where you sit.

customs.title: Shoes off, placed neatly
customs.creator: At the threshold
customs.why: Toes pointing out, ready for whoever leaves next.

customs.title: Wipe your own bowl
customs.creator: Ōryōki
customs.why: Clean it with the last of your tea and drink that too.

customs.title: Clean together
customs.creator: Sōji
customs.why: A short daily period when everyone cleans, teacher included.

customs.title: Turn toward the wall
customs.creator: Sōtō custom
customs.why: Sōtō students sit facing the wall, as Bodhidharma is said to have done for nine years.

customs.title: Walk between sittings
customs.creator: Kinhin
customs.why: Half a step for each breath, hands held at the chest.

games.title: Go
games.creator: Board game · China, Japan and Korea
games.why: Black and white stones on a grid of nineteen lines. Simple rules, no hidden information and no end to its depth. Long played in Japanese temples and counted among the arts.

games.title: Tokaido
games.creator: Board game · Antoine Bauza
games.why: You walk the old coast road from Kyoto to Edo. The winner is the traveller who savoured the most: views, meals, hot springs, encounters.

games.title: Karuta
games.creator: Card game · Japan
games.why: A hundred classical poems on cards. A reader begins a verse and players reach for the card that completes it. Played at New Year, it rewards a still mind and quick hands.

festivals.title: Rohatsu
festivals.creator: 1 to 8 December
festivals.why: A week of intensive sitting that ends on the day the Buddha’s awakening is remembered. In many monasteries it is the hardest retreat of the year.

festivals.title: Hanamatsuri
festivals.creator: 8 April
festivals.why: The Buddha’s birthday. A small statue of the infant Buddha stands in a flower-covered pavilion and visitors pour sweet tea over it.

festivals.title: Obon
festivals.creator: Mid-August, or mid-July in some regions
festivals.why: Families welcome the spirits of their ancestors home, visit graves and dance. Lanterns are floated to send them back.

festivals.title: Joya no Kane
festivals.creator: 31 December, at midnight
festivals.why: Temple bells are struck 108 times to see out the old year, once for each of the troubling passions.

places.title: Eihei-ji
places.creator: Fukui Prefecture, Japan
places.why: The mountain monastery founded by Dogen in 1244, still a working training temple of the Soto school. Visitors can join a short stay.

places.title: Ryoan-ji
places.creator: Kyoto, Japan
places.why: Fifteen stones in raked gravel, seen from the veranda. From any seat one stone is always hidden.

places.title: Daitoku-ji
places.creator: Kyoto, Japan
places.why: A walled Rinzai complex of sub-temples and gardens closely tied to the tea ceremony. A few sub-temples open to visitors.

places.title: Engaku-ji
places.creator: Kamakura, Japan
places.why: Founded in 1282, a short walk from Kita-Kamakura station. D. T. Suzuki trained here. Public sitting sessions are held.

places.title: Shaolin Temple
places.creator: Mount Song, Henan, China
places.why: The monastery where legend places Bodhidharma, the first Chan patriarch, facing a wall for nine years.

places.title: Tassajara Zen Mountain Center
places.creator: Ventana Wilderness, California, USA
places.why: Opened in 1967 as the first Zen training monastery outside Asia. Guests are received in the summer months.

ethics.title: Do no harm
ethics.text: The first of the pure precepts. Before doing good, stop doing damage: in speech, in what you consume, in how you move through a room.
ethics.practice: Catch one unkind sentence today before it leaves your mouth.

ethics.title: The bodhisattva vow
ethics.text: Beings are numberless; I vow to free them. The vow is impossible on purpose. It turns practice outward.
ethics.practice: Dedicate this morning’s sitting to one person who is struggling.

ethics.title: Not wasting
ethics.text: Nothing is yours to squander. Use what you have fully and with respect, from water to time.
ethics.practice: Finish what is on your plate and what is on your desk.

ethics.title: Right speech
ethics.text: Speak what is true, useful and timely, and otherwise be quiet.
ethics.practice: Before speaking, ask: is it true, is it kind, is it needed?

ethics.title: Not praising self, not blaming others
ethics.text: One of the ten grave precepts. Both habits keep the self at the centre.
ethics.practice: Go a day without one self-promoting remark.

ethics.title: Gratitude for labour
ethics.text: The meal verse begins: innumerable labours brought us this food.
ethics.practice: Thank one person whose work you usually do not see.

philosophy.title: Just this
philosophy.text: Nothing is missing from this moment. The search for something better is the only thing in the way.
philosophy.practice: Stop once an hour and name what is actually here.

philosophy.title: Beginner’s mind
philosophy.text: Meet each task as if for the first time, without the weight of what you already know.
philosophy.practice: Do one familiar thing today as if you had never done it.

philosophy.title: Practice and awakening are one
philosophy.text: Dōgen: you do not sit in order to become a Buddha. Sitting is what a Buddha does.
philosophy.practice: Sit today with no goal for the sitting.

philosophy.title: No separate self
philosophy.text: Look for the one who is looking. What you call the self is a stream, not a thing.
philosophy.practice: When irritated, ask quietly: who is it that is offended?

philosophy.title: Impermanence
philosophy.text: Everything that begins, ends. Seen clearly this is not sad; it is why anything can happen at all.
philosophy.practice: Watch one thing finish today: a cup of tea, a conversation, the light.

philosophy.title: Form is emptiness
philosophy.text: From the Heart Sutra. Things exist, but not on their own: each is made of everything else.
philosophy.practice: Hold a piece of bread and trace it back: baker, wheat, rain, sun.

philosophy.title: Not knowing
philosophy.text: A Chinese master said: not knowing is most intimate. Certainty closes the door that attention opens.
philosophy.practice: In one conversation, ask instead of telling.

philosophy.title: Ordinary mind is the Way
philosophy.text: Awakening is not somewhere else. It is washing the bowl, completely.
philosophy.practice: Choose your dullest chore and give it everything.

philosophy.title: The great doubt
philosophy.text: Rinzai teachers say: great doubt, great awakening. Hold the question; do not rush to fill it.
philosophy.practice: Carry one question all day without answering it.

philosophy.title: One time, one meeting
philosophy.text: This meeting, with this person, in this light, will not come again.
philosophy.practice: Give the next person you meet your whole attention for two minutes.

journal: When were you fully present today, and when were you elsewhere?
What did you do with complete attention?
What did you cling to that you could have let pass?
Describe one ordinary moment in detail.
What did silence show you?
Where did you rush, and what were you rushing toward?
What did you notice today for the first time?
What happened in your body during zazen?
Which thought came back most often on the cushion?
What did you do today that needed no improvement?
Where did you add a story to a plain fact?
What did you waste?
What did the work of your hands teach you?
Who did you meet as if for the first time?
What ended today?
When did you want the moment to be different from what it was?
What did the meal taste like?
What were you sure of this morning that you are less sure of now?
Where did you seek praise?
What sound did you hear when you stopped?
What would be different if there were nothing to attain?
Whose labour did you depend on today?
What question are you carrying?
When did you act before thinking, and it was right?
What did you clean, and how did it feel to finish?
What are you holding that is already gone?
Where was the self loudest today?
What would a beginner have seen that you missed?
What was enough?
Write three lines about this evening. Do not explain them.
reflect: What did sitting still reveal that moving had hidden?
Which practice changed you the most, and why?
Where did you resist, and what was the resistance protecting?
What does "just this" mean to you now?
What will you keep doing without counting it?

intro: Zen is a school of Buddhism built around one act: sitting down, being still and seeing directly. It distrusts explanations, including its own.

The name tells the story of its journey. The Sanskrit word for meditation, dhyāna, became chan in China and zen in Japan. Tradition traces the school to Bodhidharma, an Indian monk said to have arrived in China around the year 520 and to have sat facing a cave wall for nine years. Whatever the history behind the legend, a distinctive Chinese school had formed by the eighth century, shaped as much by Daoist plainness as by Indian scripture.

Its early masters taught by encounter rather than lecture: a shout, a question turned back on the asker, a bowl to be washed. These exchanges were collected and became kōans, cases that a student sits with until the reasoning mind gives up and something else answers. A four-line verse attributed to the school sums up its claim: a special transmission outside the scriptures, not depending on words, pointing directly at the mind, seeing one’s nature and becoming Buddha.

Two Japanese monks carried the practice home. Eisai returned from China in 1191 with the Rinzai school and with tea. Dōgen returned in 1227 with the Sōtō school and a single instruction, shikantaza: just sit. Rinzai trains with kōans and sudden breakthrough. Sōtō holds that sitting itself is awakening and that nothing needs to be added. Both run monasteries where sitting, chanting, cooking and sweeping are one continuous practice.

Because Zen treats every activity as practice, it soaked into Japanese culture well beyond the temple: ink painting, the dry garden, the tea ceremony, haiku, archery, the taste for things plain and weathered. In the twentieth century it travelled west through the books of D. T. Suzuki and through teachers such as Shunryū Suzuki, who opened a small sitting group in San Francisco in 1959.

This Onda borrows the daily shape of lay Zen practice: sit in the morning, work with attention, eat one meal in silence, end the day with tea. Zen is a living religious tradition, and nothing here replaces a teacher or a community. If the sitting takes hold, find a local group and sit with them.
guide.era: 6th century China; 12th century Japan to today

figures.name: Bodhidharma
figures.bio: The semi-legendary Indian monk counted as the first patriarch of Chan in China.

figures.name: Huineng
figures.bio: The Sixth Patriarch. By tradition an illiterate woodcutter who awakened on hearing a line of the Diamond Sutra.

figures.name: Zhaozhou
figures.bio: Tang master of the plain reply: "Mu", "Wash your bowl", "Have some tea".

figures.name: Linji
figures.bio: Fierce Tang master whose line became Rinzai Zen.

figures.name: Eisai
figures.bio: Brought Rinzai Zen and tea cultivation from China to Japan. Founded Kennin-ji in Kyoto.

figures.name: Dōgen
figures.bio: Founder of Sōtō Zen in Japan and of Eihei-ji. Author of the Shōbōgenzō.

figures.name: Ikkyū
figures.bio: Poet, abbot and scourge of pious hypocrisy.

figures.name: Sen no Rikyū
figures.bio: Tea master who gave the tea ceremony its austere, rustic form.

figures.name: Hakuin
figures.bio: Reviver of Rinzai. Organised kōan training and asked for the sound of one hand.

figures.name: Ryōkan
figures.bio: Hermit monk and poet who called himself the Great Fool.

figures.name: D. T. Suzuki
figures.bio: Scholar whose English books introduced Zen to the West.

figures.name: Shunryū Suzuki
figures.bio: Sōtō priest who founded San Francisco Zen Center and Tassajara.

history.what: Bodhidharma is said to arrive in China
history.detail: The earliest records are thin and the details are legend, but the story of nine years facing a wall at Shaolin set the tone for the school.
The Platform Sutra, composed in his name, argues that awakening is sudden and available to anyone, lettered or not.

history.what: The Tang golden age of Chan
history.detail: Mazu, Zhaozhou, Linji and Dongshan teach by direct encounter. Baizhang is credited with the first monastic rules for Chan, including daily work.

history.what: The Blue Cliff Record is compiled
history.detail: Yuanwu’s collection of one hundred kōans with commentary. A century later Wumen assembles the shorter Gateless Gate in 1228.

history.what: Eisai returns to Japan with Rinzai Zen
history.detail: He also brings tea seeds and later writes a treatise on drinking tea for health.
He writes Universal Recommendations for Zazen almost at once: the first Japanese instructions for sitting.
The temple of eternal peace, deep in the mountains of Echizen. It is still one of the two head temples of Sōtō Zen.

history.what: Zen shapes the arts of Kyoto
history.detail: Under shogunal patronage Zen temples become centres of ink painting, garden design and poetry. Ryōan-ji’s rock garden dates from the end of this period.
The tea master, ordered to take his own life by the warlord Hideyoshi, leaves behind the wabi style of tea.

history.what: Bashō sets out for the north
history.detail: His five-month walk becomes The Narrow Road to the Deep North.
From a poor country temple he trains a generation of teachers and arranges kōans into a graded course still used today.
The Rinzai abbot Shaku Sōen speaks at the World’s Parliament of Religions. His student D. T. Suzuki translates.

history.what: D. T. Suzuki publishes Essays in Zen Buddhism
history.detail: The first of the books that introduce Zen to English readers.

history.what: Shunryū Suzuki arrives in San Francisco
history.detail: Americans begin joining his dawn sittings. San Francisco Zen Center is incorporated in 1962 and opens Tassajara, a mountain monastery, in 1967.

concepts.text: Seated meditation: the core of the practice.
concepts.detail: Upright, still, eyes lowered, breathing naturally. In Sōtō it is done facing a wall with no object. In Rinzai it is often done holding a kōan.

concepts.text: A recorded exchange used as an object of meditation.
concepts.detail: A kōan is not a riddle with a clever answer. The student holds it until the habit of standing outside and analysing falls away, then shows the teacher what is left.
Rinzai emphasises a breakthrough experience; Sōtō is wary of chasing one. Both agree that an insight not lived out in ordinary conduct is worth little.
Emptiness is not nothingness. It means that every thing depends on everything else and has no fixed core, which is exactly why change and compassion are possible.

concepts.text: Every being already has the capacity for awakening.
concepts.detail: Dōgen went further and read the phrase as: all beings are Buddha nature. Practice does not create it. Practice expresses it.

concepts.text: The teaching passes from teacher to student, mind to mind.
concepts.detail: Zen lineages are written as family trees back to the Buddha. The early links are legend, but the insistence on a living teacher is real.

concepts.text: The two main schools of Japanese Zen.
concepts.detail: Rinzai: kōans, vigorous training, close work with a teacher. Sōtō: shikantaza, just sitting, and attention to the forms of daily life. A smaller third school, Ōbaku, arrived in the seventeenth century.
Chan monasteries supported themselves by farming, unlike the alms-based monasteries of India. Work was folded into the meditation schedule and stayed there.

concepts.text: The beauty of the modest and the worn.
concepts.detail: Wabi is spare simplicity; sabi is the patina of age. The tea masters prized a cracked bowl over a perfect one.
Sixteen in the Sōtō tradition: three refuges, three pure precepts and ten grave precepts, from not killing to not disparaging the three treasures.

facts.text: Zen, chan, sŏn and thiền are the Japanese, Chinese, Korean and Vietnamese readings of one character, which renders the Sanskrit dhyāna, meditation.
Dōgen was twenty-three when he sailed to China. An old monastery cook, drying mushrooms in the midday sun, taught him that the kitchen was practice too.
The rock garden at Ryōan-ji holds fifteen stones, arranged so that at least one is always hidden from wherever you sit on the veranda.
Eisai’s treatise Drinking Tea for Health opens by calling tea an elixir for nourishing life.
Hakuin’s best-known kōan is: you know the sound of two hands clapping. What is the sound of one hand?
In a Zen monastery the cook, the tenzo, is one of the six senior officers and is expected to be a mature practitioner.
Legend says Bodhidharma cut off his own eyelids to stay awake, and that the first tea plants grew where they fell.
Steve Jobs studied with the Sōtō priest Kōbun Chino Otogawa, who also officiated at his wedding.

glossary.meaning: The Chinese school from which Japanese Zen descends.
The school of just sitting, brought to Japan by Dōgen.
The school of kōan training, brought to Japan by Eisai.
Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, Dōgen’s life work.
A very short scripture on emptiness, chanted daily in Zen temples.
Buddha, Dharma and Sangha: the teacher, the teaching and the community.

learnFrom.note: The Sōtō school’s official international site, with zazen instructions and a temple directory.

learnFrom.note: Founded by Shunryū Suzuki. Online talks and beginner instruction.

learnFrom.name: A local sitting group
learnFrom.note: Zen is learned by sitting with others. Most groups welcome first-timers on a set evening each week.

sensitivity.note: Zen is a living Buddhist tradition. This Onda adapts its everyday lay practices. It is not ordination, and it does not replace a teacher or a community.
requiredCaveats: Sitting through pain is not the goal: adjust your posture or use a chair.
If meditation brings up distress that does not settle, stop and speak to a qualified teacher or clinician.
